subsection: 1. Physical and chemical changes during preparation and cooking

notes.b: A physical change alters the size, shape, state, colour or texture of food without forming new substances.
points: Coagulation: heat unfolds egg and milk proteins, which bond into a set structure, as in custard, scrambled egg and omelette.
Gelatinisation: starch granules absorb water and swell when heated, thickening sauces, gravies and custard.
Tenderising: long, moist cooking converts collagen in connective tissue into gelatine, making tough cuts of meat tender.
Shrinkage: meat loses water and melted fat during cooking, so it becomes smaller and lighter.
Increase in size: dried beans, pasta and rice absorb water and swell during cooking.

Colour change: meat turns from pink to brown or grey as its myoglobin is heated; green vegetables lose their bright colour as chlorophyll turns olive-brown in the presence of acid or with overcooking.

notes.b: A chemical change alters the molecular structure of food and forms new substances with different colours, flavours and textures.
points: Chemical raising agent: bicarbonate of soda reacts with an acid such as buttermilk and releases carbon dioxide gas, which makes soda bread rise.
Baking powder contains bicarbonate of soda and an acid, and releases carbon dioxide when it is moistened and heated.
Biological raising agent: yeast feeds on sugar during fermentation and gives off carbon dioxide, which makes bread dough rise.

notes.b: Enzymic browning is a chemical change caused by enzymes in damaged fruit and vegetables. It happens without heat.
points: Cutting, peeling or bruising breaks cell walls and lets the enzyme polyphenol oxidase meet phenolic compounds in the food.
Oxygen from the air is needed: the enzyme oxidises the phenolic compounds, which then form brown pigments.
Examples: sliced apple, banana, avocado, potato and mushroom turning brown on standing.
Acid such as lemon juice lowers the pH and slows the enzyme's action; vitamin C (ascorbic acid) reduces the first brown products back to colourless compounds.
Keeping cut surfaces under water, sugar syrup or a layer of juice excludes oxygen.
Blanching vegetables in boiling water inactivates polyphenol oxidase before they are frozen.
Refrigeration slows enzyme activity but does not stop it.

notes.h: Investigation: controlling enzymic browning on a fresh apple
points: Aim: to find which treatment best slows enzymic browning on a sliced apple.
Hypothesis: lemon juice will slow browning more than an untreated slice, because acid slows polyphenol oxidase.
Independent variable: the treatment applied to each slice, e.g. untreated (the control), dipped in lemon juice, dipped in sugar syrup, dipped in salt water.
Dependent variable: the degree of browning, rated on a 0 to 5 colour scale at fixed times.
Controlled variables: the same apple variety and ripeness, slices of the same thickness cut with the same knife, the same dipping time, the same room temperature and the same time after cutting.

Method: 1. Wash and dry the apple and cut it into slices of equal thickness. 2. Dip each treated slice for the same time, keeping one untreated slice as the control. 3. Lay all slices on labelled plates and record the colour of each every 5 minutes for 30 minutes.
Safety and hygiene: wash hands and the apple, use a clean board and a sharp knife held with a claw grip, and wipe up any spilled juice.
Expected result: the untreated control browns first and most, while the lemon juice slices stay palest for longest.
Evaluation: a rating by eye is subjective and apples vary, so repeat the test with several apples and average the ratings.

notes.b: Non-enzymic browning needs heat and does not involve enzymes. Its three processes are the Maillard reaction, caramelisation and dextrinisation.
points: Maillard reaction: amino acids from protein react with reducing sugars such as glucose when food is heated in dry conditions, producing brown colour and roasted flavour.
Maillard browning shows on roast meat and poultry skin, roast potatoes, toast and the crust of bread.
Little Maillard browning occurs in boiled or stewed food, because water keeps the surface below the temperature needed for browning.
Caramelisation: sugar melts and darkens under strong heat, forming caramel with a sweet, slightly bitter flavour; it needs no protein.
Caramelisation examples: caramel sauce, crème caramel and toffee.
Dextrinisation: dry heat breaks starch down into short-chain dextrins, which brown and give a crisp, golden surface.
Dextrinisation examples: toast, the golden top of a crumble, and the surface of baked biscuits.

notes.h: Loss of nutrients during preparation and cooking
points: Water-soluble vitamins, vitamin C and the B group, dissolve into cooking water and are lost when it is poured away.
Vitamin C is also destroyed by heat and oxidation, so the longer vegetables are cooked and exposed to air, the more is lost.
Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K are more stable in cooking but drain away with the fat from grilled or roasted food.
Minerals such as potassium and iron leach into cooking water along with the water-soluble vitamins.
Cutting vegetables into small pieces increases the surface exposed to water and air, and soaking them before cooking increases loss.
Peeling thinly or cooking in the skin reduces loss, because nutrients are concentrated just beneath the skin.
Holding cooked vegetables hot for long periods destroys further vitamin C.
Steaming, stir-frying and microwaving use little water and short cooking times, so they conserve more nutrients.
Cooking liquid from vegetables can be used in soups, sauces or gravies to recover some nutrients.

keyTerms.definition: A change that alters the appearance, size, state or texture of food without forming new substances.
A change that alters the molecular structure of food and forms new substances.
The setting of egg or milk protein into a solid structure when it is heated.
The swelling and thickening of starch granules as they absorb water and are heated.
Browning of cut fruit or vegetables caused by enzymes reacting with oxygen and phenolic compounds.
The enzyme in fruit and vegetables that causes enzymic browning when their cells are damaged.
A non-enzymic browning reaction between amino acids and reducing sugars under dry heat, producing colour and flavour.
The browning of melted sugar under strong heat, producing caramel.
The breakdown of starch by dry heat into dextrins, which brown and crisp the surface of food.
A vitamin, such as vitamin C or a B-group vitamin, that dissolves in water and is lost into cooking water.

factCards.term: Three conditions needed for enzymic browning
factCards.definition: Damaged cells releasing polyphenol oxidase, phenolic compounds in the food, and oxygen from the air.

factCards.term: Three ways to prevent enzymic browning
factCards.definition: Add acid such as lemon juice; exclude air by keeping the food under water or syrup; blanch vegetables to destroy the enzyme.

factCards.term: Two reactants in the Maillard reaction

factCards.definition: Bicarbonate of soda with an acid such as buttermilk, and baking powder.

factCards.term: Four physical changes in food during cooking
factCards.definition: Shrinkage; increase in size from water absorption; tenderising of meat; thickening from starch gelatinisation.

factCards.term: Two water-soluble vitamins lost in cooking water
factCards.definition: Vitamin C and a B-group vitamin such as thiamine.

questions.prompt: Explain how enzymic browning occurs in cut fruit and state one method of preventing it.
questions.model: Cutting or bruising damages cell walls and releases the enzyme polyphenol oxidase. The enzyme acts on phenolic compounds in the presence of oxygen from the air, oxidising them to brown pigments. Prevention, any one of: add lemon juice, whose acid slows the enzyme; keep the cut surface under water or syrup to exclude oxygen; blanch vegetables in boiling water to destroy the enzyme before freezing.

questions.prompt: Describe the physical and chemical changes that take place in food during cooking, with examples, and explain how a cook can reduce the loss of nutrients when preparing vegetables.
questions.model: Physical changes: coagulation of egg protein, as in custard; gelatinisation of starch, thickening a sauce; tenderising of meat as collagen converts to gelatine in moist cooking; shrinkage of meat as water and fat are lost; increase in size of dried beans as they absorb water. Chemical changes: Maillard reaction between amino acids and reducing sugars under dry heat, browning roast meat and toast; caramelisation of sugar, as in toffee; dextrinisation of starch, as in toast; chemical raising agents releasing carbon dioxide, as in soda bread. Nutrient loss: water-soluble vitamins and minerals leach into cooking water, and vitamin C is destroyed by heat and air. Reducing loss: cut vegetables into large pieces just before cooking; use little water and a short cooking time; cook with a lid on; peel thinly or cook in the skin; steam or stir-fry; do not hold cooked vegetables hot for long; use the cooking liquid in soups or sauces.
